Subject of this illustration: In the spring of 1928, a young engineer named Thomas Midgley Jr. stood in a laboratory in Dayton, Ohio, and demonstrated that a new synthetic gas could be breathed without harm and would not catch fire even when a lit match was held to it. The compound, dichlorodifluoromethane, soon became known as Freon-12. Within a few decades it and its chemical cousins had replaced ammonia and sulfur dioxide in millions of refrigerators and air conditioners, making safe mechanical cooling available to homes, offices, and cars around the world. Yet the same stability that made these chlorofluorocarbons so useful allowed them to drift intact into the stratosphere, where they began steadily dismantling the ozone molecules that shield Earth from ultraviolet radiation.
